decisions.rationale: The attribution context identifies Easy Mo Bee, and the extract says Puff's concept was 'to create a story line for the album,' matching the claim about Puffy's concept for 'Intro.'
The extract says, 'Biggie made it to represent Brooklyn. To show how he grew up, how we grew up,' which directly supports the claim and is attributed in the article to Lil' Cease.
The quoted passage says Biggie 'would do one voice, then come behind and do the other one later' and 'leave a gap' to fill later, matching the claimed recording method and attribution to Easy Mo Bee.
The extract is explicit: 'Biggie picked that beat in my car.' The attribution context identifies Easy Mo Bee for 'Machine Gun Funk.'
The source text says 'that beat was offered first to Big Daddy Kane,' and the surrounding context attributes the statement to Easy Mo Bee while discussing 'Warning.'
The extract describes Biggie's wording as 'his whole intensified approach' and 'an emotional expression,' supporting the claim that Easy Mo Bee framed the extreme language that way.

The extract states, 'My sister did the interlude ... with all the girls on it' and 'the other girls on it ... that's just my sister's friends,' which directly supports the claim and attribution to Lil' Cease.
The quoted source says 'Him and Lil' Kim did it' and describes a Daddy's House booth with 'the piano and the chair to the piano,' matching the claim's details and attribution to Lil' Cease.
The extract says Easy Mo Bee wrote 'The What' on the disc and that Puff responded, 'that shit is cool,' which supports both the naming and Puff's approval.
The source says, 'I used an MPC60' and 'reinforced the bass lines and drums' to give the loop 'a little more hip-hop flavor,' directly supporting the claim and attribution to Poke.
The extract states that while Digga was 'picking out the instruments' Biggie 'would make a face like, “Yeah, I want something similar to that,”' which matches the claim.
The source says the original sample was from 'a Minnie Riperton song that Stevie Wonder wrote' and that Stevie said, because of 'this cursing,' 'You can't use it,' which supports the claim.

The extract says the song was 'for Mr. Cheeks, the Lost Boyz,' that 'we gave that song to the Lost Boyz,' then 'Get that song back' and 'We traded them for another track,' matching the claim and attribution to Nashiem Myrick.

The extract says Biggie would take 'our situation or our conversation,' 'analyze it and absorb it,' and 'make a song about it,' which directly supports the claim about Banger's recollection during 'Respect.'
The extract explicitly identifies the sampled hook lyric and then says, 'That's Black Mambo,' supporting the claim that Easy Mo Bee identified the sample source for 'Friend of Mine.'
The extract plainly states, '“Unbelievable” was the final song [recorded for] Ready To Die,' matching the claim and attribution to DJ Premier.

The source says that after the character 'has shot himself,' 'the phone drops and there was supposed to be a body thud,' which supports the claim about the intended ending and attribution to Prince Charles Alexander.
The fetched-body text from Wikipedia says, 'Wallace, when interviewed, explained his “Who Shot Ya” lyrics as simply portraying a rivalry between drug dealers,' which directly matches the claim.

The Wikipedia fetched-body says the song is built on a sample of 'Blues and Pants' written by James Brown, and that 'its production was done by Ringo'; the attribution context identifies Ringo as Rashad 'Ringo' Smith.
